Royal spoonbill chicks emerge from eggs incubated for 24.5 days [ab = 24.5 days] in nests maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a developmental period typical of threskiornithid species. At hatching, these altricial nestlings weigh approximately 69 grams [Wwb = approximately 69 grams], a modest body mass that reflects the relatively small yolk reserves characteristic of spoonbill eggs. This neonatal mass is substantially lower than that observed in many other wading birds of comparable adult size, likely due to the extended period of biparental provisioning that begins immediately after hatch. The downy chicks are entirely dependent on their parents for thermoregulation and food delivery during the first several days post-hatch, with both adults alternating brooding duties and regurgitating partially digested aquatic prey into the nestlings' gaping bills. Growth proceeds rapidly under this intensive care regime, with the chicks gaining mass steadily as they develop the distinctive spatulate bill morphology that will later define their foraging technique.

Fledging, marked by the first achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest structure, occurs at 47.5 days after hatching [tx = 47.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This relatively prolonged nestling period compared to smaller-bodied Ciconiiformes reflects the time required for full development of the flight feathers and the complex bill musculature essential for tactile foraging. Following fledging, the young birds remain in close association with their parents for an additional period, during which they refine their foraging skills through observation and trial. The attainment of sexual maturity, or puberty, occurs considerably later at 142.5 days after hatching [tp = 142.5 days after hatching], a timing that allows individuals to complete somatic growth and establish the physiological condition necessary for gonadal activation at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C].

Adult body size in the Royal spoonbill exhibits pronounced sexual size dimorphism, a pattern common among many Ciconiiformes. Females reach an ultimate wet weight of 1575 grams [Wwi = 1575 grams], while their male counterparts attain a substantially greater asymptotic mass of 1886 grams [Wwi = 1886 grams]. This difference of over 300 grams reflects the selective pressures associated with male-male competition for nesting territories and the energetic demands of provisioning females during the incubation period. The acquisition of this adult body mass requires several months of sustained foraging on crustaceans, fish, and aquatic insects in shallow wetland habitats. The species' characteristic side-to-side sweeping foraging motion, facilitated by the highly sensitive spatulate bill, allows efficient prey capture in turbid waters where visual hunting would be ineffective. Maximum recorded longevity in the wild is 36.2 years [am = 36.2 years] at 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], a remarkably long lifespan for a bird of this body size and one that underscores a slow life-history strategy typical of long-lived wading birds with low annual adult mortality.

The onset of reproductive activity in Royal spoonbills is delayed relative to many other wading birds, with first breeding typically recorded at 1095 days since birth [tR = 1095 days since birth] when maintained at 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This extended pre-reproductive period allows young adults to gain the foraging proficiency and social status necessary to secure optimal nesting sites within the breeding colony. Nesting occurs in mixed-species colonies alongside other herons, egrets, and cormorants, with spoonbills typically occupying the central portions of the colony where predation risk from aerial predators is reduced. Females construct a platform nest of sticks and reeds in the canopy of mangroves or in dense reed beds, lining the structure with softer vegetation. Each breeding season, a female typically lays 2 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 3 eggs per clutch], producing a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year] at 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], reflecting the substantial energetic investment required to produce each calcareous egg and the protracted period of chick rearing that follows.

Comparative life-history analyses place Platalea regia firmly among the slower end of the avian life-history continuum, consistent with its position as a large-bodied, long-lived wading bird inhabiting unpredictable wetland environments. The energetic demands of reproduction, including the production of a single clutch of 3 to 5 eggs annually, are substantial for females that must accumulate sufficient lipid reserves prior to laying. Adult spoonbills exhibit strong site fidelity to established breeding colonies and foraging grounds, with individuals returning year after year to the same wetland systems across their range from eastern Australia to New Zealand and parts of Southeast Asia. Population monitoring indicates that recruitment rates are tightly linked to rainfall patterns and subsequent prey availability in ephemeral floodplain habitats, with breeding success fluctuating considerably between wet and dry years. The species' slow maturation and low annual fecundity, coupled with its high adult survivorship, make it particularly vulnerable to habitat degradation and wetland loss across its distribution. Conservation efforts have therefore focused on protecting key breeding colonies and maintaining the hydrological integrity of the shallow lakes and estuaries that constitute its primary foraging habitat.
